messages.content: What are the most common chords in a pop song?

function.name: music_theory_primary_triads

message.content:
In contemporary pop music the harmonic palette is surprisingly small—most hit‑makers rely on just a handful of diatonic chords (and a few predictable extensions) that create a sense of familiarity while still sounding fresh. Below is a quick guide to the “core” chords you’ll hear in almost every pop track, plus a few extra tricks that give those songs their distinctive flavor.

---

## 1. The Diatonic Triads (I–VII)

| Roman numeral | Function | Example in C Major |
|---------------|----------|--------------------|
| **I** | Tonic – home base | C |
| **ii** | Sub‑dominant minor | Dm |
| **iii** | Mediant minor | Em |
| **IV** | Sub‑dominant major | F |
| **V** | Dominant major | G |
| **vi** | Relative minor | Am |
| **vii°** | Leading‑tone diminished | Bdim |

> *Why it matters:*  
> These seven chords form the backbone of most pop progressions. Even when a song feels “outside” its key, it usually lands back on one of these diatonic shapes.

---

## 2. The Most Common Progression Patterns

| Pattern | Description | Typical Key | Example Chords (C Major) |
|---------|-------------|-------------|--------------------------|
| **I–V–vi–IV** | The “pop‑synth” or “Axis of Awesome” progression | Any major key | C – G – Am – F |
| **vi–IV–I–V** | A slight twist that starts in the relative minor | Any major key | Am – F – C – G |
| **I–vi–IV–V** | Classic “doo‑wop” feel | Any major key | C – Am – F – G |
| **ii–V–I** | Jazz‑inspired turnaround, but works in pop | Any major key | Dm – G – C |
| **I–IV–V** | Simple three‑chord loop | Any major key | C – F – G |
| **I–vi–ii–V** | “50s progression” with a jazzy lift | Any major key | C – Am – Dm – G |

> *Quick tip:*  
> In practice, pop songs often start on the tonic (I), move to the dominant (V) or its relative minor (vi), then resolve back to I. That’s why I–V–vi–IV is so ubiquitous—it gives a satisfying rise and fall without overcomplicating things.

---

## 3. Why Those Chords Work

| Feature | How It Helps |
|---------|--------------|
| **Tonic (I)** | Provides resolution and comfort. |
| **Dominant (V)** | Creates tension that wants to resolve back to I. |
| **Relative Minor (vi)** | Adds melancholy or introspection while staying close to the tonic. |
| **Sub‑dominant (IV)** | Offers a gentle pre‑dominant motion that feels uplifting. |
| **Secondary Dominants (e.g., V/V)** | Add color by temporarily borrowing from another key area. |
| **Borrowed Chords (e.g., ♭III, ♭VI)** | Inject unexpected emotion (e.g., a bright lift or a dramatic shift). |

---

## 4. Extensions & Color Notes

| Extension | When It’s Used | Example (C Major) |
|-----------|----------------|-------------------|
| **7th (major/minor)** | Adds depth; common in ballads and R&B | Cmaj7, G7 |
| **9th/11th/13th** | Gives a jazzy or soulful vibe | Am9, Fmaj13 |
| **Sus2/Sus4** | Creates suspension before resolving | Csus2, Fsus4 |
| **Add9 / Add11** | Keeps the harmony open | Cadd9, Gadd11 |
| **♭9 / #9** | Adds tension before a dominant resolution | G7♭9, G7#9 |

> *Pro tip:*  
> Pop producers often layer a basic triad with a seventh or add‑9 chord in the background to make the harmony sound richer without changing the underlying progression.

---

## 5. Practical Examples

| Song | Key | Core Progression | Notable Twist |
|------|-----|------------------|---------------|
| “Let It Be” – Beatles | C | I–IV–V | Uses a IV–V turnaround at the end of each verse. |
| “Someone Like You” – Adele | A | I–vi–IV–V | Adds a subtle ii–V turnaround before the chorus. |
| “Shape of You” – Ed Sheeran | C | I–IV–V | Uses a suspended IV (Fsus4) for added tension. |
| “Bad Guy” – Billie Eilish | C | I–vi–IV–V | Adds a G7♭9 in the bridge for a darker feel. |
| “Happy” – Pharrell Williams | C | I–IV–V | Uses a G7♯9 in the bridge for a funky lift. |

---

## 6. Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

```
Key: C Major
I   : C
ii  : Dm
iii : Em
IV  : F
V   : G
vi  : Am
vii°: Bdim

Common Pop Progressions:
I–V–vi–IV   → C – G – Am – F
vi–IV–I–V   → Am – F – C – G
I–vi–IV–V   → C – Am – F – G
ii–V–I      → Dm – G – C
I–IV–V      → C – F – G
I–vi–ii–V   → C – Am – Dm – G
```

---

### Bottom Line

If you’re writing or arranging a pop track, start with one of the six core patterns above. Keep the chords diatonic (or only borrow a few color tones), and remember that the emotional journey of a pop song is largely driven by how you move between I, V, vi, and IV. Once you master those moves, you’ll have a solid foundation for countless hits.
